ECE 6390 / Orbits and look angles

Elevation & horizon

From the figure to the physics

Fig. 1 shows how Earth-center geometry and the station’s local horizon determine elevation.

The central angle γ joins the station and satellite subpoint at Earth's center. Elevation E is measured at the station above its local horizontal. These angles have different vertices.

On a spherical Earth, E = atan2(rₛ cos γ − Rₑ, rₛ sin γ). The numerator is the outward radial component of the line of sight; the denominator is its horizontal magnitude. Here Rₑ and rₛ are geocentric radii in the same units.

The geometric horizon occurs at γₕ = acos(Rₑ/rₛ). The inverse-cosine elevation expression gives the magnitude of elevation; a visibility test can restore its sign. Terrain and atmospheric refraction require additional modeling.

Example

For the illustrative radius rₛ = 2Rₑ, the horizon lies at γ = 60°. At γ = 90°, signed elevation is atan2(−1, 2) = −26.565°.

Model and course sources

    Practice

    1. For rₛ = 2Rₑ and γ = 75°, is the satellite geometrically visible? What sign should its elevation have?

    Compare γ with acos(1/2) before evaluating any elevation magnitude.

    The horizon central angle is 60°. Since 75° exceeds it, the satellite is below the spherical horizon and its signed elevation is negative.
